pinterest.title: Guinea Fowl Korma with Toasted Almond and Green Cardamom
pinterest.description: Guinea fowl korma is what happens when Pakistani braising logic meets a French bird with something to prove. Slow-cooked pintade in a yoghurt sauce built on whole green cardamom and toasted almonds — the technique is Lahori, the bird is from the Burgundy tradition, and the result belongs to neither place entirely. Recipe at mubashirr.com

instagram.caption:
Guinea fowl has a reputation for being difficult. Lean, firm, slightly gamey — the kind of bird that punishes impatience. So I did what Pakistani cooking has always done well: I slowed it down.

A korma is not a curry in the way most people imagine. It is a braise, really. The yoghurt goes in cold, the heat is low, and the fat separates out slowly — that moment chefs call bhunna — before the liquid is reintroduced. Green cardamom, a handful of blanched almonds toasted until they colour, a restrained hand with the spice. Nothing here is aggressive.

The pintade, which is what the French call this bird, takes to korma treatment remarkably well. The slow braise pulls the fibre apart without drying it. The almond thickens the sauce and softens it at the same time.

I have been cooking across these two traditions long enough to know when a combination earns its place and when it is just novelty. This one earns it.

Recipe is on the blog. Link in bio.

email.subject: Guinea Fowl Korma is on the Blog
email.preheader: Pakistani braising logic applied to a French bird. It works — here is why.
email.body_html:
Guinea fowl is not a forgiving bird. It is lean where chicken is generous, firm where it needs to be coaxed, and it carries a faint wildness that demands the cook pay attention.

Which is exactly why korma suits it.

A proper korma is a study in patience. The yoghurt goes in cold, the heat stays low, and you wait for the fat to separate before you do anything else. That moment — the bhunna — is where the flavour is built. Rush it and you have a thin sauce. Give it time and you have something else entirely.

For this version, I used whole green cardamom, blanched almonds toasted until they take on colour, and a yoghurt sauce that thickens as it reduces. The pintade — which is simply what the French call this bird — has been a staple of Burgundian cooking for centuries. It turns out it has been waiting for this treatment all along.

The technique is Pakistani. The bird is French. The result is neither a novelty nor a compromise. It is a dish that makes a clear argument for itself on the plate.

Full recipe, method, and notes on sourcing halal guinea fowl are on the blog.

linkedin.body:
Two culinary traditions share more than most people assume.

Korma — the Pakistani braising method built on cold yoghurt, low heat, and patience — is structurally closer to a French braise than it is to what most restaurants label a korma. Both rely on fat separation before liquid is reintroduced. Both treat time as an ingredient.

When I applied this method to guinea fowl — a bird the French have prized for centuries precisely because its leanness rewards slow cooking — the logic held immediately.

The result is a guinea fowl korma with green cardamom and toasted almonds. The yoghurt sauce develops the way it should: slowly, with the fat rendering out before the spice is bloomed into it. The almonds are blanched, then toasted, then incorporated to thicken the sauce without starch.

What interests me about this kind of work is not the novelty of the combination. It is the discovery that two traditions, developed separately across centuries, arrived at similar conclusions about how heat and time transform protein.

That is not fusion for its own sake. It is technique recognising technique.

I have written the recipe and the reasoning behind it here: https://mubashirr.com/guinea-fowl-korma-almond-cardamom/

A korma is a braise before it is anything else. Cold yoghurt, low flame, patience. You wait for the fat to separate — that is the bhunna — and only then do you move forward. Rush it and the sauce never recovers.

Guinea fowl, or pintade as the French call it, has been a Burgundian staple for the same reason it works here: the muscle responds to slow heat. The fibre loosens. The slight wildness of the bird becomes a quality rather than a problem.

Whole green cardamom. Blanched almonds toasted to colour. A yoghurt sauce that thickens on its own. No shortcuts, no stock, no workaround. Just Pakistani technique applied to a French bird and the patience to let it work.
